7334c5b0a253f0211e1a8c9f76666c0c4fdf75db.note: This in-silico analysis of CCND1 (Cyclin D1) SNPs identifies four missense variants potentially destabilising the protein and links high CCND1 expression to reduced breast-cancer survival. Relevance to this thesis is partial: it engages with breast-cancer biology and variant-effect prediction (Polyphen2, SIFT, PROVEAN), so it could be cited in Chapter 1's breast-cancer section or as methodological precedent for predicting functional consequences of missense variants in the MCF-7 WGS work in Chapter 5. It does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress or fragile sites.

446ca565d71b7fd7d1c84c2898f73cffcee17a2a.note: AURORA's multi-omics profiling of 381 paired primary/metastatic breast tumours is directly relevant to this thesis: it documents enrichment of driver mutations (ESR1, PTEN, PIK3CA, RB1) and clonality changes between primary and metastasis, and shows that high tumour mutational burden in HR+/HER2- disease predicts shorter relapse. Useful for Chapter 1's tumour-evolution and clonal-variations section (1.9) and the genome-wide WGS framing of Chapter 5. Provides a benchmark cohort against which the smaller MCF-7 WGS findings can be discussed.

25ef5dad03a7ff7f729dbd2f53ecb1fbb4582bde.note: General review of breast-cancer biomarkers covering nucleic-acid, protein and cellular markers, including circRNAs and miRNAs as diagnostic candidates. Useful as a broad citation for Chapter 1's breast-cancer overview (1.2) when motivating the search for genomic biomarkers, but the review does not engage with ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites or the WGS mutational-burden framing that drives this thesis. Treat as background/context citation rather than mechanistic support.

aad85b7121b5d348fc49b8476ae3b502f528ce91.note: Foundational review reframing R loops from transcription byproducts to drivers of chromosome fragility and genome instability. Highly relevant to this thesis's replication-stress framing: ZFP36L1's role as an AU-rich-element RNA-binding protein places it close to the cotranscriptional R-loop literature, and predecessor work by Sidali (2023) in the same lab established R-loop accumulation at FRA14C in ZFP36L1-/- cells. Should be cited in Chapter 1's DNA-replication/replication-stress sections (1.12, 1.14) and revisited when interpreting genome-instability findings.

1459f37cf04e30db07f4c4b435a58fe9c4632941.note: Mechanistic study showing the Polϵ proofreading exonuclease and CTF18 cofactor act with PARP1 to prevent replication-fork collapse at single-ended DSBs caused by leading-strand encounters with single-strand breaks. Directly relevant to this thesis's replication-stress and DNA-damage-response themes (Chapter 1, sections 1.12-1.14): clarifies how forks fail and how fork-reversal pathways relate to HDR. Provides a current mechanistic citation that complements the older aphidicolin literature on stalled forks and licensing factors.

614259152d7fe4ee1f7c37530909bba354e2c24e.note: Review of DNA-damage-response defects in breast cancer and the resulting therapeutic vulnerabilities (platinum, PARP inhibitors, immunotherapy). Relevant to Chapter 1's section linking breast cancer to the DDR (1.8): supports the rationale that DDR pathway status shapes both carcinogenesis and treatment response. Less mechanistic than Aguilera 2012 or Ahmad 2023, but a useful clinically-oriented citation for situating the MCF-7 WGS work within the wider breast-cancer DDR landscape.

f6a781a0b4af0b3a313ea5fd6a19e38461dff0d1.note: Argues that positive selection on zinc-finger proteins in undifferentiated stem cells shaped mammalian adaptive evolution, suggesting these proteins acquired new transcriptional-regulation functions over time. Relevance to this thesis is thematic rather than mechanistic: ZFP36L1 is a zinc-finger RNA-binding protein, but this paper concerns evolutionary genetics of zinc-finger transcription factors rather than ZFP36L1 specifically or its replication-stress role. Could be cited in passing in Chapter 1's ZFP36L1 introduction (1.10) for the broader ZFP family context.

b85b1de4edc8954c3f670afe05c724086334db0a.note: Machine-learning analysis of prostate-cancer RNA-Seq identifying transcripts (HEATR5B, DDC, GABPB1-AS1) as candidate biomarkers. Marginally relevant to this thesis: the disease focus (prostate) and modality (transcriptomics, not WGS) sit outside the breast/osteosarcoma + WGS scope, and there is no engagement with ZFP36L1 or replication stress. Could be cited only as methodological precedent for NGS-derived biomarker discovery in Chapter 1's WGS-in-cancer section, but stronger options exist.

d022aefbea344df7e5912d9961e34da7997f640f.note: Review of S100 calcium-binding proteins in cancer, covering their roles in proliferation, apoptosis, inflammation and links to breast cancer, lung cancer and melanoma. Tangential to this thesis: S100 proteins are mechanistically unrelated to ZFP36L1 and were not identified as candidate hits in the MCF-7 or U2OS WGS top-mutated lists. Inclusion would only be warranted if a Chapter-5/6 candidate gene turns out to be an S100 family member; otherwise it can be omitted.

6cfe2d42afcf3e88fd62f3ef19a834445e70135c.note: Review of antitumour and proinflammatory immune responses in breast cancer, including immunotherapy strategies. Tangential to this thesis's genomic-instability focus, but provides broader breast-cancer biology context for Chapter 1's section 1.2 if the discussion touches on how genomic alterations interact with tumour-microenvironment immunity. No direct engagement with ZFP36L1 (which has well-documented immune-cell roles via mRNA decay) or with replication stress; could be cited if Chapter 1 broadens to immune-microenvironment context.

fcbb1b4c40158b198f471e88a2de59c6ae47a17e.note: Reviews the dual enhancer/promoter potential of regulatory DNA elements and the determinants of their transcriptional outputs. Relevance to this thesis is contingent: it becomes useful in Chapter 1's WGS sections (1.14, 1.15) when motivating interpretation of variants in non-coding regulatory regions, and in Chapter 5/6 if any candidate variants are found within enhancer or promoter elements. Not directly applicable to ZFP36L1 or replication-stress mechanism, but valuable for interpreting the non-coding mutational landscape.

02f3c4db03315c9379ab06d83c99abaebf24f161.note: Identifies CDT1, the DNA-replication licensing factor, as a candidate oncogene whose overexpression accelerates S-phase entry and is tumorigenic in NIH3T3 cells. Directly relevant to Chapter 1's section 1.12 on DNA replication and pre-replication-complex licensing: CDT1 dysregulation is a paradigmatic source of replication stress and re-replication, complementing cyclin-E and MCM-loading discussions already cited. Provides historical-mechanistic grounding for why licensing-factor imbalance matters in cancer and links cleanly to the aphidicolin/fork-stalling literature.

e574cc196f7bdec4d7843d5f9f8d0adb36411663.note: Landmark study showing that aphidicolin-induced replication stress in normal human cells generates copy-number changes across the genome that mechanistically resemble both polymorphic CNVs and disease-associated CNCs, with breakpoint microhomology pointing to NHEJ or template-switching repair. Directly relevant to this thesis: pre-dates and motivates the MCF-7 and U2OS WGS experiments — Arlt provides the in-vitro proof that aphidicolin treatment produces precisely the kind of variants this thesis sequences for. Cite in Chapter 1's replication-stress sections (1.12-1.14) and Chapters 5/6 when interpreting CNV calls in aphidicolin-treated samples.

a905ea4fbe7fd74ea35f41da33b1f7c39fc721cd.note: Reviews how variation in non-coding regions and DNA methylation regulates HLA Class I/II gene expression, with implications for immune-related disease. Limited direct relevance to this thesis: HLA genes were not flagged in MCF-7 or U2OS top-mutated lists, and the thesis does not address tumour immunology. Could be cited in Chapter 1's WGS section if the discussion of non-coding-variant interpretation explicitly draws on HLA as an example, but stronger non-coding citations are likely available.

c4193bf31366b2f29b9a86e6d527e718a6d9c7cb.note: Reviews the MMTV-PyMT transgenic mouse as the most-used genetically engineered model of breast cancer, mapping its histological and molecular progression onto human disease. Useful for Chapter 1's animal-models-of-breast-cancer section (1.3) where mouse models are surveyed alongside other organisms. Does not engage with ZFP36L1 or replication stress, and the MCF-7/U2OS cellular models in this thesis are in vitro, but the citation supports broader rigour about how breast-cancer model systems compare.

291a485a9408d00a50a590679f816b542f25b20a.note: Recent review surveying precision-oncology methodologies — rapid sequencing, single-cell, spatial mapping, epigenetics, liquid biopsies — and their application to tumour heterogeneity, non-coding variation and inherited risk. Useful general citation for Chapter 1's WGS-in-cancer-research section (1.15) and Chapter 7's cross-lineage synthesis: it provides an up-to-date framing of how cancer genomics has matured beyond simple mutation calling. No direct ZFP36L1 or replication-stress engagement, but a strong methodological-context reference.

58678e273846d27976c636b917e27f03cb0d6076.note: Reviews physical and psychological functioning of older cancer survivors compared with non-cancer age-matched groups; concludes survivors fare worse on both dimensions but the literature is limited. Not relevant to this thesis's biological/genomic focus: there is no thematic overlap with ZFP36L1, replication stress, WGS or any cellular model used here. Recommend removal from the bibliography unless cited elsewhere in the thesis for a section the audit hasn't covered (e.g. a discussion of clinical implications in Chapter 8).

627819d0d9182c9963504b77cfab2f0691839892.note: Reviews the bottlenecks preventing WGS uptake in routine clinical microbiology, including strain identification, virulence and resistance profiling, and transmission-chain reconstruction. Relevance to this thesis is largely methodological and adjacent: the clinical-microbiology framing differs from cancer genomics, but the review's discussion of WGS workflow, data interpretation and 'theory to practice' translation gaps maps cleanly onto the clinical-WGS section of Chapter 1 (1.14-1.15). Useful for situating cancer WGS within the broader picture of how genomics moves from research into clinical decision-making.

2ee73a694920d064e00721eb26af6f33f67ddf19.note: Whole-exome sequencing of 206 multi-region samples from 68 colorectal cancers documents extreme intratumour heterogeneity with a Darwinian evolution pattern, divergent left- vs right-sided CRC trajectories, and polyclonal lymph-node and extranodal deposits. Disease-context differs from this thesis (CRC vs breast/osteosarcoma), but the methodological framing — multi-region sequencing, ITH, single-biopsy limitations — is directly transferable to Chapter 1's tumour-heterogeneity section (1.9) and to Chapter 7's cross-lineage discussion. Note this is a bioRxiv preprint; check whether a peer-reviewed version has since appeared before citing in the final thesis.

aa0f68226b3289f826b46a4dec36ff7c2fc88ae0.note: Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing of 103 + 22 breast cancers (a landmark of the modern WGS-in-breast-cancer era) confirms PIK3CA / TP53 / AKT1 / GATA3 / MAP3K1 recurrence, identifies recurrent CBFB mutations + RUNX1 deletions, and discovers a MAGI3-AKT3 fusion enriched in triple-negative disease. Directly foundational for Chapter 1's tumour-evolution (1.9) and breast-cancer genomics (1.2) sections, and for Chapter 5's MCF-7 WGS framing — Banerji 2012 is one of the obvious benchmark cohorts to discuss the MCF-7 mutation calls against. Note this is the canonical paper now correctly resolved post-merge.

bbe021fae60ed38eb26eb7dde1756620630df990.note: Identifies a new class of fragile sites — early-replicating fragile sites (ERFSs) — distinct from classical late-replicating CFSs, co-localising with highly-expressed gene clusters in B cells under replication stress. Important conceptual extension of the fragile-site literature directly relevant to Chapter 1's CFS section: the thesis is built around aphidicolin-induced replication stress at fragile loci (FRA3B, FRA14C), and Barlow's work shows fragility is not limited to late-replicating CFSs. Cite in §1.12-1.13 and in Chapter 6 when discussing whether U2OS variants concentrate at classical CFSs versus other fragile-site classes.

0f5a2c574938a435a0df4ce34229fd9cc254d9e4.note: Reviews how Ca2+ pumps and channels — including CFTR-related currents — contribute to tumorigenesis via mechanisms independent of bulk cytosolic Ca2+ transport. Tangential to this thesis's genomic-instability focus, but useful for Chapter 5 if any of the MCF-7 candidate genes (e.g. CLCN3, highlighted in the project notes) turn out to be ion-channel members. The review's framing of channel-mediated migration / invasion / proliferation provides context for interpreting ion-channel variants surfacing in the MCF-7 WGS top-mutated list.

5b23d60c1b55316fcc1f3459f5ec3c5299de51a3.note: Concise review of Chk1 and Chk2 checkpoint kinases as signal transducers of genome-integrity surveillance, candidate tumour suppressors, and therapeutic targets. Foundational reference for Chapter 1's DNA-damage-response sections (1.8, 1.13-1.14): together with the Bartkova 2005/2006 papers it forms the canonical DDR-checkpoint citation cluster that the replication-stress narrative of this thesis depends on. Brief and well-cited; the obvious citation when introducing ATR-Chk1 / ATM-Chk2 in the aphidicolin context.

ac14138a1a66c23dab20825c77f071e4a66aa92a.note: Landmark observation that early human precursor lesions (bladder, breast, lung, colon) constitutively activate an ATM/ATR-Chk2-p53 DNA-damage response, with the response acting as an inducible anti-cancer barrier suppressed by checkpoint defects in progression to malignancy. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's DDR / oncogenic-stress sections (1.8): provides the clinical-tissue evidence that replication stress is engaged during human tumour initiation. Should be cited alongside Bartkova 2006 and Bartek 2003 when motivating why aphidicolin-mimicking replication stress is a relevant disease model.

cbdf053a769db2d5ecedfa42ae466fbbd5ea7ab8.note: Companion paper to Bartkova 2005 showing that oncogene-induced senescence is mechanistically linked to replication-stress-induced DNA double-strand breaks, with ATM kinase activity required for the senescence response. Directly relevant to Chapter 1's discussion of replication stress as a tumorigenesis barrier (1.8, 1.12) — together Bartkova 2005 and 2006 establish that the replication-stress / DDR-senescence axis is engaged in human pre-cancerous tissue. Provides the mechanistic bridge from aphidicolin-style replication stress in cells to the in-vivo precursor-lesion observations.

ee1adf2329b3b81a01ca4c748ad616f6e335c926.note: UK population-based study of 94 male breast cancer cases that quantified BRCA1 / BRCA2 contributions: no BRCA1 carriers found, around 8% BRCA2 carriers, accounting for only 15% of excess familial risk in female first-degree relatives — implicating yet-undiscovered BC-risk genes. Tangential to this thesis's focus: useful only as an epidemiology/genetics citation in Chapter 1's breast-cancer sub-section (1.2) where male BC is mentioned, or to motivate the search for non-BRCA breast-cancer susceptibility genes. Consider whether a more recent population study would serve the same purpose.

5cb9a32018cc1966092aad8165e925b353392348.note: First identification of WWOX, a gene spanning the chromosome 16q23.3-24.1 region commonly affected by allelic losses in breast cancer, mapping to the FRA16D common fragile site. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's CFS section: WWOX/FRA16D is one of the canonical large-gene/CFS pairings (alongside FHIT/FRA3B), foundational for the thesis's framing that fragile sites are coupled to large tumour-suppressor genes. Cite in §1.12-1.13 when introducing CFS biology, and revisit in Chapter 5/6 if any candidate-gene hits map to WWOX or other FRA-spanning loci.

53ea382c4cf9294c4330fc7d17f270ff4161e0e1.note: Mouse-genetics paper showing Zfp36l1-/- embryos die mid-gestation with vascular and placental defects driven by elevated VEGF-A — and crucially, that ZFP36L1 controls VEGF-A through translational regulation rather than mRNA decay. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's ZFP36L1 section (1.10): one of the early in-vivo demonstrations that ZFP36L1 has essential developmental roles, and one of the few papers showing translational (rather than purely decay-based) regulation by this RNA-binding protein. Anchors the broader biology behind why ZFP36L1 loss might have genome-wide consequences in MCF-7 / U2OS.

bf9c451403a809e4ed04a0d987db360b123dce9c.note: Pan-cancer analysis of focal somatic copy-number alterations across 3,131 specimens identifying 158 recurrently altered regions, of which 122 lack a known cancer-driver gene — and demonstrates dependency of cancer cells on amplified MCL1 / BCL2L1 anti-apoptotic genes. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's WGS / mutational-burden sections (1.14-1.15) and Chapter 5/6 CNV analyses: provides the canonical pan-cancer CNA atlas against which the MCF-7 and U2OS CNV calls can be discussed. Particularly useful for distinguishing 'driver-explained' from 'fragile-site-explained' deletions / amplifications.

1be0114c9f32f06d0b64b7a676618e1dba6f9ebe.note: In vitro / in vivo / in silico study of fullerene C60 nanoparticles on DMBA-induced rat mammary tumours, showing apoptosis induction (caspase-3 up, Bcl-2 down) and inhibition of MCF-7 viability. Tangential to this thesis's genomic-instability focus: the MCF-7 cell-line connection is the only thematic overlap, and the mechanism (nanoparticle toxicity) is unrelated to ZFP36L1 or replication stress. Could be cited only as an MCF-7-related background paper if Chapter 1's breast-cancer treatment overview discusses experimental therapeutics. Otherwise, not core.

d27b1c0102399e41524fdd21c57af30967162115.note: Review of how obesity drives oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer via aromatase regulation in breast adipose stromal cells, including pro-proliferative oestrogen signalling and endocrine-therapy resistance in post-menopausal women. Relevant to Chapter 1's breast-cancer section (1.2) when discussing modifiable risk factors and hormone-receptor biology. Not connected to this thesis's replication-stress / ZFP36L1 focus, but provides a useful general citation for breast-cancer aetiology and the population-level context in which MCF-7 (an ER+ line) sits as a model system.

7325a051e764fd6689a7b9ca68e159d594c81af4.note: Identifies 2,428 somatic homozygous deletions across 746 cancer cell lines and derives structural signatures distinguishing tumour-suppressor-driven from fragile-site-driven deletions; shows 11% of protein-coding genes are dispensable for human cell survival. Foundational for Chapter 1's WGS / fragile-sites sections (1.12-1.15): provides the analytical framework for telling 'biologically meaningful' from 'inherently fragile' deletion calls — directly applicable to the MCF-7 / U2OS CNV interpretation in Chapters 5-6. The 746-cell-line panel also contains MCF-7 and U2OS for benchmarking.

4ef4550b423190505bbeb25bd5b937344cb2730a.note: Shows that impaired DNA replication in haematopoietic progenitors paradoxically promotes leukaemogenesis by giving Bcr-Abl- or mutant-p53-expressing cells a competitive advantage that requires replicative stress to manifest. Conceptually important for Chapter 1's replication-stress-as-cancer-driver framing (1.12, 1.14): provides in-vivo evidence that impaired DNA replication selects for oncogenic events. Connects directly to the aphidicolin model: chronic mild replication stress in this thesis's MCF-7 / U2OS systems mirrors the conditions Bilousova shows favour pre-malignant clone expansion. Useful for the discussion of why aphidicolin selects ZFP36L1-/- vulnerabilities.

ffea49fd98e314c0cb3a727ba4df536ab46c989c.note: Minireview of how p53, p73 and HIPK2 link DNA-damage signalling to apoptotic and autophagic responses, with particular focus on nuclear-body signalling. Relevant to Chapter 1's DDR section (1.8) as a citation for how the canonical DNA-damage axis decides between repair, arrest and cell death. Not directly engaged with replication stress or fragile sites; useful as a general DDR-to-apoptosis citation rather than a mechanistic anchor. Bartek 2003 and Bartkova 2005/2006 are likely more load-bearing for the same conceptual real estate.

571d12e327d4de832b72c65ec002573060d1bf51.note: Shows that low transcription destabilises large genes at common fragile sites while strong transcription paradoxically stabilises them by triggering an earlier replication-timing switch. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's CFS / replication-stress sections (1.12-1.13): refines the dominant 'transcription-replication conflict = fragility' model and complements the R-loop literature (Aguilera 2012, Sidali 2023). For Chapter 5/6 it offers a framework for interpreting why some large genes (FHIT, ROBO2) are recurrently mutated under aphidicolin in this thesis's WGS data: it is about replication-timing context, not just transcription level.

b9d18c0112be7a476a6889f0fce6b731c2d0cf0a.note: Reviews G-quadruplex secondary DNA structures, their conservation across genomes, and the role of their formation / resolution in genome integrity and transcriptional regulation. Tangential to this thesis: G4-DNA is a known contributor to replication stalling and fragile-site fragility, so it sits adjacent to the CFS / replication-stress story but is not directly engaged in this thesis's experimental design. Useful as a 'mechanism' citation in Chapter 1's DNA-replication section (1.12) if discussion of non-B-form DNA contributions to fork stalling is included; otherwise omittable.

f983efb3576ec42887e0be39d4da4dad24e869b8.note: Review of how mitochondrial dynamics (fission / fusion, biogenesis, mitophagy, spatial regulation) are modulated by oncogenes and tumour suppressors, with knock-on effects for cell cycle, metabolism and stress response. Tangential to this thesis's nuclear-genome focus, but useful in Chapter 5 if the MT-ND5 variant findings in MCF-7 are discussed — that section of Chapter 5 specifically calls out an MT-ND5 hit, and Boland 2013 provides the broader mitochondrial-dysfunction-in-cancer context for interpreting why mitochondrial-encoded variants might appear in the WGS top hits.

1a22461f339c7c3ed0fa88c9948efd14c0b66577.note: Foundational paper showing that CRISPR spacer sequences in prokaryotes derive from extrachromosomal elements (mostly phages) and that S. thermophilus phage sensitivity correlates inversely with spacer count — hypothesising the adaptive-immunity model of CRISPR. Highly relevant to Chapter 1's CRISPR-history section (1.5): one of the canonical pre-Cas9 papers that established the biological function of CRISPR systems and motivated the subsequent decade of engineering work. Cite when tracing the chronology from Ishino 1987 to Jansen 2002 to Bolotin 2005 to current CRISPR/Cas9 applications.

082d28ad121aff666d91cc2554f211d59e69f515.note: Reviews the role of ion channels in cancer-cell apoptosis evasion and how channel-mediated control of life/death decisions could be therapeutically exploited. Relevance to this thesis is contingent on the candidate-gene story in Chapter 5: if CLCN3 (a chloride channel previously flagged in the MCF-7 candidate list) becomes a featured deep-dive gene, Bortner 2014 is a useful citation linking channel biology to apoptotic regulation in tumours. Otherwise tangential. Pair with Barrett 2014 if both are needed for a coherent channel-and-cancer paragraph.

80dca1658795b647ec90f3303c70a73889c1638f.note: Biochemical study of how mitochondrial-encoded ND4 and ND5 subunits contribute to NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase (complex I) assembly in human cells, showing that loss of ND4 or ND5 dislodges the 24 kDa nuclear-encoded subunit from the inner membrane. Directly relevant to Chapter 5 §5.4.4 MT-ND5: if the MCF-7 WGS calls a recurrent MT-ND5 variant, Bourges 2004 provides the mechanistic context for why ND5 loss / disruption matters for complex-I integrity — supporting any functional-relevance argument about MT-ND5 as a candidate gene.

736fff359eff88f6f0a13087c5eea328b0699209.note: GLOBOCAN 2018 cancer incidence and mortality estimates: 18.1 million new cases and 9.6 million deaths globally in 2018, with breast cancer the most common cancer in women and the leading female cause of cancer death. Standard epidemiology citation for Chapter 1's opening (chapter preamble and §1.2 Breast Cancer) when motivating the global burden of breast cancer. Not mechanistic; pure population-level framing. Consider whether a more recent GLOBOCAN year is preferable for the final thesis.

98d499d09492eece27af1c0ea46b1056026ce4d2.note: Case report of Leigh syndrome caused by the MT-ND5 m.13513G>A mutation, presenting with WPW-like conduction defect, cardiomyopathy and hyponatraemia at 12 months of age, with 50% mutation load in muscle / lymphocytes. Directly relevant to Chapter 5 §5.4.4 MT-ND5 if the MCF-7 WGS flags m.13513G>A or similar disease-associated mitochondrial variants: Brecht 2015 establishes the clinical pathogenicity of this specific position and so calibrates expectations about whether MCF-7 MT-ND5 variants represent disease-associated or somatic / passenger calls.

97d7f8db5a22380dce62e581a74e133b0bab8436.note: Review of breast-cancer prevention strategies including population-level risk-factor reduction and precision prevention via validated risk-assessment models (polygenic risk, mammographic density) and risk-reducing medication. Relevance to this thesis is largely contextual: useful for Chapter 1's §1.2 Breast Cancer overview when discussing why breast-cancer incidence remains a public-health concern despite growing biological knowledge. Not directly engaged with ZFP36L1 or replication stress; consider citing if Chapter 8 (general discussion) touches on translational implications of CRISPR / genomics-based risk stratification.

32eb4a025cfd981e9c38f07bd44df7f4cbb6238b.note: Review of the three-way relationship between replication-timing programmes, replication stress and genomic instability, including in cancer. Highly relevant to this thesis: provides an up-to-date framing of how replication timing modulates which loci are vulnerable to aphidicolin-induced stress — directly applicable to Chapter 1's §1.12 DNA-replication / §1.13 aphidicolin / §1.14 WGS-and-genome-instability sections. The replication-timing angle complements Blin 2019 (transcription-replication interplay) and connects to the broader question of why certain large genes accumulate variants under chronic replication stress.

6dbc096f6422fc3ba2ef7c3eb80b2c153f09df5e.note: Nature Protocols paper introducing LDAcoop, an R-based tool for limiting-dilution-assay (LDA) analysis of clonogenic cells incorporating non-linear population dynamics. Methodological citation only; not directly engaged with ZFP36L1, replication stress or WGS biology in this thesis. Could be cited if Chapter 4 (chemosensitivity / cell-survival assays) used LDA-format experiments. Otherwise minimal relevance — consider whether the citation supports a specific assay choice in this thesis or is reference-list clutter.

c71755706b5c4238f382c22da3f4fb8cfd41f8c7.note: Recent review on WGS integration into clinical practice covering rare-disease genomics, oncogenomics, pharmacogenomics and the move into long-read / single-cell / nanopore technologies. Useful for Chapter 1's §1.14-1.15 WGS-in-cancer-research sections as an up-to-date framing of where clinical WGS is heading. Pairs well with Avci 2025 (precision-oncology methodology review) and Balloux 2018 (clinical WGS bottlenecks) to motivate the broader importance of WGS-derived findings beyond the immediate ZFP36L1 question.

81a98cdeac7dd8de0d69ec5293bcbee90a79b2af.note: Review of zinc-finger proteins (ZNFs) in neurological and psychiatric disease, summarising ZNF classes and their pathophysiological roles. Tangential to this thesis's focus: ZFP36L1 is mentioned in the broader ZNF family context, but the paper's clinical scope is neurological rather than oncological. Could be cited very briefly in Chapter 1's §1.10 ZFP36L1 introduction as background on the breadth of zinc-finger protein biology beyond the cancer literature, but a more cancer-focused ZNF review would serve better. Probably omittable.

ac94561e12652bf86151ac0dce47ec75fb95c8f6.note: Current Protocols overview of DNA microarray technology, its history and how it has been progressively superseded by next-generation sequencing. Useful as a methodological footnote in Chapter 1's §1.14-1.15 WGS sections when contrasting microarray-based discovery with WGS-derived variant detection, or in Chapter 5/6 Methods if any aspect of microarray-derived expression data is incorporated as supporting evidence. Otherwise tangential — this thesis is WGS-centric and microarray context is mostly historical.

1d641a29ecfca2a6de6f04ac5b405d74b54b144e.note: Review of breast-cancer treatment by molecular subtype (luminal A/B, HER2-enriched, TNBC), endocrine and anti-HER2 therapies, and emerging immunotherapy / conjugated-antibody approaches. Relevance to this thesis is general-context: useful in Chapter 1's §1.2 Breast Cancer overview when situating MCF-7 (an ER+ model) within the broader treatment landscape and for any discussion of the clinical importance of subtype-specific genomic alterations. Not mechanistic with respect to ZFP36L1 or replication stress; treat as background citation.

d1391d581b935d8d007672d0d675c0c2df9a5313.note: Perspective arguing that oestrogen-receptor signalling in hormone-dependent breast cancer converges to suppress DDR effectiveness (ATM, ATR, CHK1, BRCA1, p53) in favour of proliferation, with implications for how cancers process oestrogen-induced DNA damage and respond to anti-hormone therapy. Relevant to Chapter 1's §1.8 (breast cancer + DDR) and §1.2 (oestrogen biology) when motivating why MCF-7 (an ER+ line) is a useful model for studying DNA-damage responses. Provides the ER-signalling-versus-DDR framing that complements the more mechanistic Bartek / Bartkova citations.

cb43daec9d0847600e18ce9ff18b2a1aed5c7319.note: Reviews the MDM2-p53 axis in hepatocellular carcinoma, framing how viral and metabolic risk factors disrupt this feedback loop to drive HCC initiation and progression. Tangential to this thesis's breast / osteosarcoma WGS focus. Could be cited if Chapter 1's §1.8 DDR discussion needs a broader p53-dysregulation example beyond breast cancer, but stronger options exist. The MDM2-p53 mechanism is well-covered by other citations in the thesis bibliography already; treat as optional background rather than load-bearing.

36595a1938e8f6e01a8ac89bc9cfa08891e18991.note: Broad review of transcriptional regulation and its misregulation in human disease. The abstract retrieved is essentially a stub (introductory paragraph only), so detailed relevance assessment is limited. Likely useful as a generic citation for Chapter 1's regulatory-element / non-coding-variant framing (§1.14-1.15) if Khalid needs a high-level review on how transcriptional dysregulation contributes to disease. Not mechanistic with respect to ZFP36L1 or replication stress. Consider replacing with a more targeted regulatory-element citation (e.g. Andersson 2020) if space is constrained.

0f15d7543a389b738781f2d0ce8c4b296c15c098.abstract: Replication stress, a hallmark of pre-cancerous and cancerous lesions, is characterised by the slowing or stalling in replication fork progression and the consequent failure to preserve genomic stability. ZFP36L1, a member of the ZFP36 family of CCCH tandem zinc finger (ZF) proteins, is an RNA-binding protein that plays a crucial role in the post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression underlying physiological processes and pathological diseases. Recent evidence has revealed that ZFP36L1 is significantly mutated or downregulated in certain human cancers, and exhibits tumour-suppressive properties across various cancer cell types. However, the precise molecular link between ZFP36L1 and cancer, particularly from the angle of genomic stability, remains poorly elucidated. Here, we report a novel role for ZFP36L1, characterised in human U2OS and U2OS H2B-GFP osteosarcoma cells, in suppressing replication stress-induced genomic instability. We found that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of ZFP36L1 resulted in increased chromosome segregation defects including anaphase bridges, chromosome laggards and micronuclei formation, even in the absence of exogenous replication stress. Moreover, ZFP36L1-deficient cells exhibited an elevated accumulation of γH2AX, 53BP1 nuclear bodies (NBs) and RPA, indicating an active role for ZFP36L1 in limiting replication stress-induced DNA damage. Furthermore, we demonstrated an unanticipated function for ZFP36L1 in potentially suppressing the expression of common fragile sites (CFSs) in response to replication stress, reflected by the increased mitotic CFS-characteristic chromosomal aberrations and MiDAS events at CFS loci observed in ZFP36L1-deficient cells. Finally, we also showed that a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated truncation in ZFP36L1, carrying a compromised lead-in sequence to its first ZF-domain, resulted in increased replication stress-associated phenotypes, similar to that of a ZFP36L1-knockout. Taken together, our data reveal, for the first time, a role for ZFP36L1 in contributing to the protection of genomic integrity against replication stress.
0f15d7543a389b738781f2d0ce8c4b296c15c098.note: Solaiman generated the U2OS ZFP36L1-/- cellular system (and a truncated lead-in/first-ZF-domain variant) by CRISPR/Cas9 and showed that ZFP36L1 loss produces chromosome-segregation defects (anaphase bridges, laggards, micronuclei), elevated γH2AX/53BP1/RPA foci, and — critically for this thesis — increased mitotic CFS-characteristic aberrations and MiDAS events at common fragile sites. This is the foundational U2OS work that Chapter 6 directly builds on: the four U2OS WGS samples (WT-U, WT-A, G3-U, G3-A) trace back to the G3 ZFP36L1-/- clones Solaiman characterised cytologically. Intellectual lineage to cite: where Solaiman observed CFS-MiDAS phenotypes by microscopy, this thesis tests whether those CFS loci accumulate WGS-detectable mutations under aphidicolin. The Chapter 6 WGS therefore stands as the molecular-genomic complement to Solaiman's cytological characterisation — same clones, complementary readout.

a1212f2c326ca5b5e77cd1073200e8a442c06038.abstract: The RNA binding protein (RBP) ZFP36L1, which binds to adenylate/uridylate (AU)-rich elements (AREs) (AU-RBP) in the 3' untranslated region of many messenger RNAs, has been extensively characterised for its role in post-transcriptional control of gene expression and is reported as a newly identified cancer driver gene. Replication stress (RS) threatens DNA replication fidelity and stability of the genome. Recently, a small number of AU-RBPs have emerged as key figures in the maintenance of genome integrity through mechanisms that govern the replication stress response and DNA repair. Herein, we report that treatment with low doses of aphidicolin results in hallmarks of RS-associated genomic instability in a cellular model depleted of ZFP36L1 using CRISPR/Cas9. We find that loss of ZFP36L1 results in defects in mitosis leading to chromosome segregation errors and genomic instability. Remarkably, we also identify loss of ZFP36L1 increases the prevalence of FANCD2-associated anaphase ultra-fine bridges indicating chromatid non-disjunction at intrinsically labile common fragile site loci. Furthermore, we detected an increase in RPA and γH2AX foci in S/G2 cells indicative of replication stress-induced DNA damage potentially indicating chronic replication fork stalling and double-strand break formation as demonstrated by increased γH2AX foci colocalising with 53BP1. Surprisingly, chromatin enrichment of U-2OS, HCT116 and HeLa cells demonstrated that ZFP36L1 is physically bound to chromatin fractions. Here we also demonstrated the specificity of CRISPR-Cas9 mediated ablation of ZFP36L1 through the inducible expression of ZFP36L1 that demonstrated suppression of 53BP1 nuclear bodies (NBs) and micronuclei formation. Importantly, we demonstrate, by overexpression of a catalytically inactive mutant of human RNase H1 tagged with GFP, that loss of ZFP36L1 induces R-loop formation. We also implicate unscheduled R-loop formation as a potential cause for replication stress-associated genomic instability through the expression of wild-type RNase H1 which was able to limit the occurrence of 53BP1 NBs in G1 phase cells and RPA in S/G2 phase cells. Finally, we highlight potential ZFP36L1 interactions through mass spectrometry that uncover proteins involved in the maintenance of genome integrity and R-loop resolution. Taken together, our work highlights an important, yet previously unidentified role for ZFP36L1 in preserving genomic stability including limiting the formation of R-loops in response to replication stress.

17119477dc5880063e701ee6206e435fa8f13669.abstract: ZFP36L1 is an RNA-binding protein which functions as a mRNA-decaying protein through binding to the adenylate-uridylate rich elements (AREs) located in the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of mRNAs, thereby mediating mRNA decay. ZFP36L1 has emerged as a breast cancer driver gene, exhibiting tumour-suppressing properties. Notably, ZFP36L1 has been reported to be significantly mutated and downregulated in various tumour types. In our comprehensive study, we identified the novel role of the ZFP36L1 gene in regulating the tumorigenic traits of breast cancer, with a particular focus on hormone-positive and HER2-negative breast cancer subtypes. Furthermore, our research explored the therapeutic potential of ZFP36L1 in combination with tamoxifen, an antiestrogenic drug used as a standard treatment for the luminal breast cancer subtype. To explore functional aspects of ZFP36L1, we generated a CRISPR/Cas9-derived knockout of ZFP36L1 in the MCF-7 breast cancer cell line, characterised by luminal A molecular subtype. Functional assays demonstrated that the loss of ZFP36L1 in MCF-7 cells reduced the cell migration capacity and reduced cell population in the G1 phase of the cell cycle. Subsequent RNA-sequencing study and western blot analysis revealed that ZFP36L1 absence leads to upregulation of cell-cycle-related genes, including cyclin D1, CDK6 and tumour suppressor p53. Notably, cyclin D1 and CDK6 transcripts contain ARE sequences in the 3' UTR, suggesting that they could be the direct targets of ZFP36L1 in MCF-7 cells. Similarly, we observed an upregulation of several ARE-rich genes associated with cell migration and extracellular matrix in the absence of ZFP36L1 in MCF-7 cells. These findings collectively illustrated that ZFP36L1 might be crucially involved in regulating key oncogenic transcripts encoding cell migration and extracellular matrix in MCF-7 cells. Our study also reported that ZFP36L1 depletion reduced the response of MCF-7 cells to tamoxifen, a standard drug used in endocrine therapy. Specifically, while tamoxifen treatment decreased the cell migration capacity of MCF-7 cells, this effect was mitigated by the loss of ZFP36L1. Western blot analysis further confirmed that tamoxifen treatment reduced cyclin D1 expression in MCF-7 cells. Conversely, when ZFP36L1 expression was inhibited, the tamoxifen-induced reduction in cyclin D1 expression was decreased, resulting in increased cyclin D1 levels compared to tamoxifen-treated wild-type counterparts. Moreover, ZFP36L1 knockout MCF-7 cells exhibited higher IC50 values than WT MCF-7 cells. Conclusively, using molecular and transcriptomic approaches, our study convincingly demonstrates that ZFP36L1 exerts control over transcripts encoding key tumorigenic traits in MCF-7 cells and highlights the potential of synergistically combining ZFP36L1 with tamoxifen, offering potential treatment opportunities for hormone-positive breast cancer subtypes.

The thesis showed that ZFP36L1 loss in MCF-7 reduces migration and G1 fraction; upregulates cell-cycle drivers cyclin D1 and CDK6 (both bearing 3'UTR AREs and therefore plausible direct ZFP36L1 targets) plus p53; broadly elevates ARE-rich migration / ECM transcripts; and reduces tamoxifen sensitivity (higher IC50, blunted tamoxifen-induced cyclin-D1 suppression). The CFS-flanking allelic deletions with POLQ signatures also inform variant interpretation in Ch5 and Ch7's comparative synthesis.

It does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, or cancer biology. Cite solely to establish HRNR's normal biological role before discussing the significance of variants detected in the MCF-7 WGS dataset.

Does not address ZFP36L1, CFSs, or specific cell-line biology.

This mechanistic detail supports Ch1 §1.12 (DNA replication and replication stress) and §1.14 (WGS and genome instability), and provides a molecular rationale for the structural variants and CNV patterns interrogated in Ch6 and Ch7.

Also pertinent to §1.8 (BC and DDR) and Ch8 discussion of why ZFP36L1 loss—an RNA-binding protein regulating transcript stability—may exacerbate transcription–replication conflicts. Does not address ZFP36L1, CFSs, or WGS directly.

It could appear as a historical background citation in Ch1 §1.5 (CRISPR discovery history) but is not essential; a later landmark paper (e.g. Jinek 2012 or Doudna/Charpentier) would be more appropriate.

Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, fragile sites, or WGS. MCF-7 and U2OS are not mentioned. Background citation at most for §1.11; not required for any experimental chapter.

Does not address ZFP36L1, aphidicolin, CFSs, or the MCF-7/U2OS cell lines; background citation only to contextualise replication stress as a cancer-promoting mechanism.

It does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, fragile sites, or genomic instability; background citation only, or omit.

d06fdb11c21a9935ce82c6e786e006704768be1f.note: Partial relevance, limited to the CLCN3 candidate-gene subsection in Ch5. However, the study focuses on ovarian cancer, not breast cancer, and does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, or fragile sites. 557e4e01b1a3cbfb613b7a7a69eb30ec14443b28.note: This paper concerns mass spectrometry-based proteomics of skin structures (corneocytes, keratin profiles, nail plate, hair shaft) and has no meaningful connection to any thesis theme. The appearance of HRNR (hornerin), a cornified-envelope protein, in the Ch5 MCF-7 candidate-gene list (§5 HRNR subsection) is the only conceivable link, but this paper offers no cancer-relevant mechanistic insight. 205d18a97b2e8451eaa023e24f512e326ea0bf29.note: Review of the biological factors driving metastatic recurrence in breast cancer, including dormancy and late relapse following surgery or systemic therapy. Relevance to this thesis is limited to general breast-cancer context: useful as a background citation in Ch1 §1.2 when framing the clinical significance of genomic instability in breast cancer and the importance of understanding disease progression in MCF-7 as a model. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, fragile sites, or WGS; treat as background citation only.

71236a0f45d66fd8dda03f8d79a8ef64ddd86f3c.note: This review of activity metabolomics and the metabolome's influence on genome, epigenome, transcriptome, and proteome has no direct relevance to this thesis. 688c0898b6009ae0e284567fbac422eab3418555.note: Proteomic characterisation of exosomes from MDA-MB-231 and MCF-10A cell lines, identifying GLUT-1, GPC-1, and ADAM10 as candidate breast-cancer biomarkers. This thesis does not examine exosomal biology, extracellular vesicles, or proteomic biomarker discovery, and the cell lines studied (MDA-MB-231, MCF-10A) are not MCF-7 or U2OS. No engagement with ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or WGS. Tangential to all thesis themes; omit or, at most, treat as a background citation in Ch1 §1.2 if a brief mention of breast-cancer biomarker research is warranted.

3fa31a65de51cc07a343a348244bc72e5572ea38.note: Directly relevant to Ch1 §1.10 (ZFP36L1). Tristetraprolin (TTP/ZFP36) is the founding member of the ZFP36 family to which ZFP36L1 belongs; both share the tandem zinc-finger ARE-binding domain and destabilise overlapping sets of oncogenic mRNA targets. This review's account of how suppressed TTP expression promotes tumorigenic phenotypes via ARE-containing transcripts provides essential mechanistic context for explaining why ZFP36L1 loss may similarly de-repress pro-tumourigenic targets. Also relevant to §1.9 (tumour evolution) given the discussion of senescence. Does not address replication stress, fragile sites, or WGS.

0fa6896ae54124c4d44668e4c765c3523fad8bb6.note: Directly relevant to Ch1 §1.10 (ZFP36L1 / RNA-binding protein biology). Demonstrates that Tristetraprolin (TTP/ZFP36), the founding member of the ZFP36 family to which ZFP36L1 belongs, is transcriptionally suppressed by Myc and functions as a tumour suppressor in B-cell lymphoma; restoring TTP impairs lymphomagenesis and abolishes the malignant state. Establishes the broader principle that ZFP36-family mRNA-destabilising proteins regulate ARE-containing oncogenic transcripts and are subject to selection pressure for loss during malignant progression — context essential for motivating why ZFP36L1 loss is studied in MCF-7 and U2OS.

68be763aebe54242b3242437e72181b120ed735d.note: Regional epidemiological and clinical characterisation of BRCA1/2 germline mutations in a Spanish cohort, reporting mutation detection rates, recurrent variants, and comparative survival outcomes in hereditary versus sporadic breast and ovarian cancer. Relevance to this thesis is peripheral: it touches on breast-cancer biology and germline variant interpretation broadly relevant to Ch1 §1.2, but addresses hereditary BRCA-associated disease rather than somatic replication-stress-driven genomic instability, ZFP36L1, or fragile sites. MCF-7 is a sporadic ER+ line with no BRCA1/2 deficiency context here. Background citation only, or omit.

1eb09f781aa78155e1571962a20ea7c7ba329e7e.note: This review of liquid chromatography stationary phases for compound separation has no relevance to this thesis. Omit from the bibliography entirely.

45522bf0be057cc8d2031ca32bf114a217622cf0.note: Review of endocrine-resistance mechanisms in ER+ breast cancer, covering ESR1 mutations, coactivator/corepressor alterations, cell-cycle regulator modulation, and approved CDK4/6, mTOR, and PI3K inhibitors. Relevance to this thesis is limited to general context: MCF-7 is an ER+ luminal model, so this review could be cited briefly in Ch1 §1.2 when characterising the clinical significance of ER+ disease and the genomic instability associated with endocrine resistance. It does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, fragile sites, or WGS methodology; treat as background citation only.

0508759355b19703658c65fa7348a2f32c1f1fb8.note: Comprehensive review of the tristetraprolin family (ZFP36, ZFP36L1, ZFP36L2) as post-transcriptional regulators that bind AU-rich elements in 3′-UTRs to promote mRNA decay, with tumour-suppressive roles across multiple cancer types. Directly relevant to Ch1 §1.10 (ZFP36L1 biology) as a primary reference for contextualising ZFP36L1's mechanism of action, its aberrant expression in cancer, and its association with prognosis, metastasis, and chemotherapy resistance. The coverage of hallmark cancer traits regulated by TTP-family members also supports §1.1. Does not address replication stress, CFSs, or WGS methodology.

b5d0a50fb624afc9657d1a6df7cc89416a120e37.note: This study concerns S100A4-mediated regulation of MMP-9 and invasiveness in prostate cancer cell lines, with no connection to ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, common fragile sites, MCF-7, U2OS, or whole-genome sequencing. The cancer type, biological mechanisms, and experimental focus are all outside the scope of this thesis. Omit from the bibliography entirely; there is no chapter or subsection for which this paper provides relevant background.

28a0dd1b74daa244978501324978b2b96a87c0b0.note: General review of intronic SNPs and their role in disease susceptibility via splicing disruption and epigenetic regulation. Relevance to this thesis is minimal: it provides no discussion of ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or the MCF-7/U2OS models. It could theoretically serve as background for interpreting intronic variants identified in the WGS data (Ch5/Ch6), but more authoritative and specific variant-interpretation literature exists. Recommend omission or, at most, a background citation if intronic SNPs are explicitly discussed during variant filtering.

532948e5ec283c2984912509b6a9e8eb476cf281.note: Demonstrates that chemotherapy (paclitaxel, gemcitabine) induces HIF transcriptional activity in multiple breast-cancer lines, including MCF-7, enriching breast cancer stem cells via IL-6/IL-8 signalling and multidrug-resistance upregulation. Relevance to this thesis is peripheral: MCF-7 is used here as a comparator ER+/PR+ line rather than a primary model, and the focus is on hypoxia-driven chemoresistance rather than replication stress, ZFP36L1, or genomic instability. Could serve as background context in Ch1 §1.2 when discussing MCF-7 biology and TNBC heterogeneity, but does not warrant substantive citation.

fda4bd6fe3c878105078b60b914753eff3a63f85.note: Prospective feasibility study demonstrating that WGS can replace or substantially extend standard-of-care molecular diagnostics in routine clinical oncology, identifying actionable biomarkers in 71% of metastatic-cancer patients and uncovering 49 previously undetected germline variants. Relevant to Ch1 §1.15 (WGS in cancer research) as clinical validation that WGS delivers comprehensive genomic profiling beyond targeted panels. Useful background for framing the thesis's own WGS approach in MCF-7 and U2OS cells. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or cell-line biology; background citation only.

311a788ca720fcbc4b3fe30b8888a0234fdaf9b6.note: Concise review of aneuploidy and chromosomal instability (CIN) as drivers of tumour heterogeneity, drug resistance, and macroevolutionary karyotypic change. Relevant to Ch1 §1.9 (tumour evolution) and to Ch6–Ch7, where CNV landscapes from WGS of ZFP36L1-deficient U2OS and MCF-7 clones are interpreted in the context of clonal evolution and genomic instability. Provides conceptual framing for why segmental copy-number alterations detected under aphidicolin-induced replication stress may have evolutionary consequences. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress mechanisms, or fragile sites directly; cite as supporting evolutionary framework rather than primary mechanistic source.

f6eee8bfd6cca556a42d87569a17fc49bccf33f9.note: This review covers KRAB-zinc finger proteins (KRAB-ZFPs) and their co-factor KAP1 in epigenetic repression via heterochromatin formation, with focus on adaptive immune cell differentiation. Relevance to this thesis is tangential: ZNF180, a KRAB-ZFP, appears as a candidate gene in the MCF-7 WGS data (Ch5), and a brief mention of KRAB-ZFP biology as transcriptional repressors could contextualise that subsection. The paper does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or cancer genomics. Recommend background citation only within Ch5's ZNF180 subsection, if at all.

454f9c745c90b5596a9a3c68a6a1e36cfb2d8f45.note: Concise review of CFS biology directly relevant to multiple thesis themes. The characterisation of CFSs as replication-stress-induced hotspots for breakage and rearrangement, preferentially unstable in pre-cancerous lesions, underpins the rationale for aphidicolin treatment in the experimental design (Ch1 §1.13) and the CFS-overlap analyses in Ch6. The finding that CFS instability is tissue- and oncogene-specific is particularly pertinent to the comparative MCF-7 vs U2OS framework in Ch7, where cell-line-specific fragile-site vulnerability is a key interpretive consideration. Foundational citation for Ch1 §1.12–1.13 and Ch6 CFS-overlap subsections.

cf54fc7a7d6c883b4c6ce55ea7a5dc92904fdf77.note: Directly relevant to the CFS biology underpinning Ch6 and Ch7. This preprint identifies a fragility signature combining replication stress-induced delay in replication timing (RT) of early/mid S-phase regions with active transcription of large genes — precisely the features associated with FRA3B/FHIT and other CFSs examined in the U2OS WGS data. The finding that RT delay under replication stress (aphidicolin-like conditions) enables mapping of novel fragile sites beyond cytogenetic detection strengthens the rationale for using WGS to identify CFS-overlapping structural variants in Ch6's CNV/CFS-overlap subsections. Cite in Ch1 §1.12–1.13 and Ch6.

64b09e2a8dde2afb964fe686e320f63b6c4b8107.note: Broad review of NGS platforms, throughput, variant-detection capabilities, and emerging analytical challenges. Relevant to Ch1 §1.14–1.15 as general background for introducing WGS methodology and its application to cancer genomics, including the mutational-burden and genome-instability analyses central to Chapters 5–7. However, the review is technology-survey rather than mechanistic: it does not address replication stress, ZFP36L1, fragile sites, or the specific bioinformatic pipelines used in this thesis. Treat as background citation when contextualising the rationale for WGS as the chosen discovery platform; not a primary reference for any analytical chapter.

3b5f5299ec7279a791e87ca4de22b09a86111f91.note: Demonstrates that BRCA1 loss exacerbates oestrogen-induced DNA double-strand breaks and genomic instability in breast cells, partly through derepression of oestrogen-metabolising enzymes (CYP1A1). Relevant to this thesis at Ch1 §1.8 (breast cancer and DDR) as contextual evidence that DDR-deficient backgrounds amplify endogenous genotoxic stress in breast tissue, paralleling the rationale for studying ZFP36L1 loss under aphidicolin-induced replication stress in MCF-7 cells. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or WGS; treat as supporting background citation rather than a central reference.

9924e9de0b0ad7239cf98c7cf39885e182f8c126.note: Comprehensive review of replication stress sources, cellular impacts, and detection assays, making it foundational for Ch1 §1.12 (DNA replication and replication stress). Directly underpins the thesis rationale for using aphidicolin as a replication-stress inducer (§1.13) and contextualises the genomic instability observed in WGS data from both MCF-7 and U2OS lines (Ch6–Ch7). The overview of detection assays is also useful when justifying WGS as a readout of replication-stress consequences (§1.14). Does not address ZFP36L1, CFSs, or specific cell lines used in this thesis.

05b68d18364cdeaee6230677ba5a0511c0d7eaaf.note: Methodological review of top-down proteomics for identifying and quantifying proteoforms via intact-protein mass spectrometry. This paper has no meaningful connection to the core thesis themes of ZFP36L1 biology, replication stress, aphidicolin, common fragile sites, WGS, CRISPR, or breast/osteosarcoma cell-line biology. Unless the thesis includes a proteomic component not reflected in the chapter map, this paper should be omitted entirely rather than cited as background.

b2c663572ae9572629eccd1aac1545c903f8e54d.note: Spatial and molecular profiling of the tumour immune microenvironment in HER2+ primary and metastatic breast cancers, demonstrating reduced immune activation at metastatic sites. There is no engagement with RNA-binding proteins, DDR, fragile sites, or CRISPR methodology. At most a background citation in Ch1 §1.2 for breast cancer heterogeneity; omission is equally defensible.

1dcea5dc27d1c24b609f8a6671caf8a99c496373.note: Mechanistic study of MYC transcriptional dysregulation via cancer-specific super-enhancers that dock onto a conserved CTCF site upstream of the MYC promoter; dCas9-DNMT epigenetic editing is used to validate the mechanism. Tangential to this thesis: MYC amplification or dysregulation may appear incidentally in the MCF-7 or U2OS WGS data, and the dCas9 methodology has loose kinship with CRISPR applications discussed in Ch1 §1.5–1.7, but the paper does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, fragile sites, or aphidicolin. Background citation only, if cited at all.

8ae16b5d27049d3ce0fbecb3af2014a0af270466.note: Concise review of the molecular basis of common and rare fragile sites (CFSs), covering their induction under partial replication stress, chromosomal gap/constriction formation, and involvement in tumour rearrangements. Directly relevant to Ch1 §1.12–1.13 and the CFS-overlap subsections in Ch6, where the mechanistic rationale for aphidicolin-induced CFS instability must be established. Provides foundational definitional and mechanistic grounding for discussing FRA3B, FRA14C, and other CFSs identified in the U2OS WGS data. Should be cited alongside Glover (2005) and Durkin & Glover (2007) as a core CFS reference.

d50e1fa6d111fb671c184374559da64dabaddd0c.note: This biochemical characterisation of S100A5, a brain-restricted EF-hand calcium-, zinc-, and copper-binding protein, has no meaningful connection to any thesis theme. Relevant to this thesis at a general-context level: the combination of CRISPR and WGS it advocates mirrors the experimental logic of using CRISPR-generated ZFP36L1-knockout clones followed by WGS (Ch1 §1.5–1.7, §1.14–1.15). Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, or fragile sites specifically. Suitable as a background citation in §1.7 or §1.15 to contextualise the CRISPR-then-sequence approach; not foundational to any core thesis argument.

However, the paper does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, or WGS methodology. Recommend background citation only if the CFS-overlap at 3p is explicitly discussed; otherwise omit.

Relevant to Ch1 §1.12 (DNA replication and replication stress) as mechanistic context for how aberrant origin licensing generates structural chromosomal aberrations analogous to those sought in the WGS data. Also supports §1.9 (tumour evolution) by illustrating how replication-derived instability cooperates with p53 loss to drive clonal outgrowth. Not directly concerned with ZFP36L1, aphidicolin, CFSs, MCF-7, or U2OS; background citation only.

4317b0b930d75a29b2ec4ccc79ab58ab967638b6.note: Partially relevant preprint examining TTP (tristetraprolin / ZC3H7, the founding member of the ZFP36 family to which ZFP36L1 belongs) as an RNA-binding protein in breast cancer subtypes, including MCF-7 cells. The finding that TTP expression varies by molecular subtype and is epigenetically regulated by chemotherapy agents provides useful comparative context for Ch1 §1.10 (ZFP36L1 biology), where the broader ZFP36 family and its tumour-suppressive roles should be introduced. Does not address ZFP36L1 directly, replication stress, fragile sites, or WGS; treat as supporting background citation rather than a primary reference.

c87067fdb714d9a8d75164843a3dc539f73fd61b.note: Landmark WGS-based study demonstrating that primary TNBCs display a continuous spectrum of clonal and mutational evolution at diagnosis, with clonal frequencies of driver mutations (TP53, PIK3CA, PTEN) varying widely across cases. Directly relevant to Ch1 §1.9 (tumour evolution / clonal dynamics) and Ch7–Ch8 when contextualising the clonal heterogeneity observed in ZFP36L1-knockout MCF-7 and U2OS WGS data. Also pertinent to Ch1 §1.15 (WGS in cancer research) as a methodological precedent for somatic mutation quantification. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, or aphidicolin; MCF-7 is ER+, not TNBC, so breast-cancer relevance is partial.

26deaff45acbc10c9861babbdeb44709d307843a.note: Directly relevant to multiple thesis themes. This study characterises aphidicolin- and hydroxyurea-induced copy number alterations (CNAs) at single-cell resolution, demonstrating that replication stress generates both focal CNAs and chromosome-arm-scale losses in a cell-type-specific manner linked to large gene expression and replication timing. Foundational for Ch1 §1.12–1.13 (replication stress and aphidicolin) and Ch6's CNV/CFS-overlap subsections, where analogous CNA landscapes are interpreted in ZFP36L1-/- U2OS cells. The observation that different replication stress inducers produce distinctive CNA signatures also informs Ch7's comparative MCF-7 vs U2OS synthesis.

Relevant to Ch1 §1.3–1.4 (animal and 2D/3D models) when justifying the use of MCF-7 monolayer cultures as an in vitro system and acknowledging their limitations relative to more complex models. The coverage of tumour heterogeneity also provides background for Ch1 §1.9. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, or WGS; treat as background citation for the cell-model rationale sections.

Background citation only; no direct engagement with ZFP36L1, replication stress, or fragile sites.

The 4T1 murine model and exosome-focused mechanism share no direct connection to any core thesis theme. Omit from the bibliography; no chapter or subsection benefits from this citation.

Relevance to this thesis is limited to general background: useful in Ch1 §1.2 when contextualising the genomic landscape of breast cancer and the clinical rationale for WGS-based approaches. Does not address ZFP36L1, replication stress, aphidicolin, fragile sites, or MCF-7 biology specifically; treat as background citation only.

This review covers ZFP36L1 explicitly as one of eight AU-rich element RNA-binding proteins (AU-RBPs) and examines both canonical mRNA-decay roles targeting DDR transcripts and non-canonical responses to genotoxic stress, including post-translational modifications and sub-cellular relocalisation. Foundational for Ch1 §1.10 (ZFP36L1 biology) and §1.8 (BC + DDR), providing mechanistic rationale for why ZFP36L1 loss may compromise genome integrity under aphidicolin-induced replication stress. Should also be cited in Ch8 when contextualising the WGS mutational burden observed in ZFP36L1-knockout clones.

1a902441a73d8ef1d981410da695c6378bf6a6c1.note: Epidemiological report providing 2019 US cancer incidence and mortality projections, noting declining death rates and persistent socioeconomic disparities. Relevance to this thesis is purely contextual: useful as an opening citation in Ch1 §1.1 (hallmarks/cancer burden) or §1.2 (breast cancer epidemiology) to establish the clinical scale of the disease and motivate the research.
